questions.q: Why is checkpointing described as the prerequisite for any restart decision?
options: Without saved snapshots of model weights, optimizer state, and scheduler state, there is no earlier point to roll back to when a restart is warranted
Checkpointing is only relevant after training completes
Checkpointing automatically fixes loss spikes
Checkpointing is only needed to save GPU power
questions.explain: A restart means resuming from a saved snapshot. Without frequent checkpoints saved to durable storage, there is nothing to roll back to, making the restart decision moot.

questions.q: What is the clearest, most unambiguous signal that a restart is warranted?
options: The learning rate is in its decay phase
Non-recovering divergence -- loss and gradient norm spike and fail to return to their prior trend within a reasonable window
MFU is slightly above its usual average
Training has been running for more than a week
questions.explain: Non-recovering divergence is the clearest trigger: once loss/gradient norm spike and stay up well past a reasonable recovery window, every further step wastes compute, so the run should be rolled back.

questions.q: Besides a sharp loss spike, what is another pattern that can justify a restart?
options: Training loss decreasing slightly faster than expected
MFU staying perfectly flat for the entire run
A gradual upward drift in gradient norm over thousands of steps, or evaluation loss diverging from training loss over an extended period
The optimizer using the Adam algorithm
questions.explain: Softer signals like a persistent gradient-norm drift or a widening gap between evaluation and training loss can indicate a developing problem even without one dramatic spike.

questions.q: When the root cause of an instability event looks systemic (e.g., the peak learning rate is clearly too aggressive for this phase), what's the typical resume strategy?
options: Always restart the entire schedule from step zero
Ignore the issue and let training continue unchanged
Switch the model architecture entirely
Resume from the checkpoint before the event, often with a slightly lowered learning rate going forward, rather than restarting from scratch
questions.explain: For a systemic cause like an overly aggressive learning rate, teams typically resume from the last good checkpoint with an adjusted (usually lowered) learning rate, reserving a full restart from step zero for rarer, corpus-wide issues.

questions.q: Why might a team deliberately choose to "let it ride" rather than restart after a loss spike?
options: Because restarting is always free and has no downside
Because checkpoints are never reliable enough to restart from
Because loss spikes never recur once ignored

Because a single-step spike that recovers within a reasonable window, with gradient norm back in its normal band, is often just noise from an atypical batch, and restarting for every such event wastes more compute than it saves
questions.explain: A brief spike that self-corrects is usually benign noise. Restarting for every minor, self-recovering blip would waste more compute (via reload overhead and lost progress) than simply continuing.
